




<!-- --- -->

<!-- **Why do we put the `ts <- ...` simulation code inside the `ts_replicate()` block? -->
<!-- What happens when you only run the `ts_f4()` command in the `{ ... block ... }` -->
<!-- inside `ts_replicate()`?** -->

<!-- ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false} -->
<!-- ### Click to see the solution -->

<!-- Let's run the `ts_replicate()` without (internally) simulating the tree sequence: -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- df_bad <- ts_replicate(n = 10, { -->
<!--   ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"]) -->
<!-- }) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- When we do this, we can see that we got the same value throughout! This is because -->
<!-- all replicates are computed on the same outcome of a single evolutionary process -->
<!-- which generated the tree-sequence object `ts`. -->

<!-- This is unlike the correct way of using `ts_replicate()`, which simulates an -->
<!-- independent `ts` object for each replicate, each of those then being based on an -->
<!-- independent realization of the demographic model in question. -->

<!-- ::: -->







Let's do a bit more $f$ statistics exploration by switching to a more
interesting example model---something that's much closer to many models used in
practical research.

**Create a new script called `introgression.R`, add the following code to it,
then run it. Looking through the model and inspecting its visualization, you'll
probably recognize a familiar sketch of ancient human history:**

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

library(ggplot2)

outgroup <- population("outgroup", time = 6200000, N = 10000)

anc      <- population("ancestor", time = 6000000, N =  1000, parent = outgroup, remove = 599999)

neand    <- population("Neanderthal", time = 600000, N =  1000, parent = anc)

san      <- population("San",      time =  600000, N = 10000, parent = anc)
mbuti    <- population("Mbuti",    time =  350000, N = 10000, parent = san)
yoruba   <- population("Yoruba",   time =  220000, N = 10000, parent = mbuti)
dinka    <- population("Dinka",    time =  150000, N = 15000, parent = yoruba)

nonafr   <- population("nonAfr",   time =   70000, N = 3000,  parent = dinka)

model0 <- compile_model(
  populations = list(outgroup, anc, neand, san, mbuti, yoruba, dinka, nonafr),
  generation_time = 30
)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model0, times = 0, list("each", 10))

plot_model(model0)

# trick we haven't seen yet: ts_names() also accepts models and schedules!
# to give us the names of "individuals to be simulated in the future from this model
s <- ts_names(model0, split = TRUE, schedule = schedule)
```

(It will become clear soon why we use the suffix `0` for the `model` and `ts`
variables.)

---

```{r}
df0 <- ts_replicate(
  10,
  {
  ts <- msprime(model0, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>% ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["San"], X = s["Mbuti"], Y = s["Neanderthal"], Z = s["outgroup"]),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["San"], X = s["Yoruba"], Y = s["Neanderthal"], Z = s["outgroup"]),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["San"], X = s["Dinka"], Y = s["Neanderthal"], Z = s["outgroup"]),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["San"], X = s["nonAfr"], Y = s["Neanderthal"], Z = s["outgroup"])
  )
  }
)

ggplot(df0, aes(f4, statistic)) +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red")
```


```{r}
gf1 <- gene_flow(from = neand, to = nonafr, proportion = 0.03, start = 55000, end = 50000)
model1 <- compile_model(
  populations = list(outgroup, anc, neand, san, mbuti, yoruba, dinka, nonafr),
  gene_flow = gf1,
  generation_time = 30
)

gf2 <- gene_flow(from = nonafr, to = neand, proportion = 0.03, start = 55000, end = 50000)
model2 <- compile_model(
  populations = list(outgroup, anc, neand, san, mbuti, yoruba, dinka, nonafr),
  gene_flow = gf2,
  generation_time = 30
)
```

```{r}
  plot_model(model1, proportions = TRUE),

)
```

## Exercise: Estimating ancestry proportions












## Exercise: How many unique f4 quartets are there?

When playing with $f$-statistics in this chapter, you've probably noticed
various symmetries in $f_4$ (but also other $f$-statistics) depending on the
arrangement of their "configuration" (order of populations). As a trivial
example, an $f_3(A; B, C)$ and $f_3(A; C, B)$ will give you exactly the same
value.

**Try to figure out, how many unique $f_4$ values involving a single quartet
(our p1, p2, p3, and p4 populations) are there. How about how many absolute
values? You can answer this either by drawing and doodling on paper, but freel
free to also use computer simulations if you'd like!**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| message: false
library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

library(slendr)
init_env()

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

# install a combinatorics R package:
# install.packages("combinat")
library(combinat)

# these are the four samples we can create quartet combinations from:
quartet <- c("p1_1", "p2_1", "p3_1", "p4_1")

# this is how we can generate all permutations:
quartets <- permn(quartet)
quartets

# how many permutations there are in total?
#   4! = 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 24
factorial(4)

# we should therefore have 24 different quartet combinations of samples
length(quartets)

# loop across all quartets, computing the corresponding f4 statistic
all_f4 <-
  map_dfr(quartets, function(q) ts_f4(ts, q[1], q[2], q[3], q[4])) %>%
  arrange(abs(f4))

# print all f4 values
print(all_f4, n = Inf)

# narrow down the results to only unique f4 values
distinct(all_f4, f4, .keep_all = TRUE)

# narrow down the results to only unique absolute f4 values
distinct(all_f4, abs(f4), .keep_all = TRUE)
```

:::

## Exercise: Mutations versus branches

Do you recall how I told you earlier that you don't have to add mutations to
your tree sequence `ts`, and still be able to compute population genetic
statistics? But that you can safely add them with `ts_mutate()` anyway?

The reason this works is because some very smart people figured out a
mathematical [duality between mutation-based and branch-based
statistics](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/215/3/779/5930459)---it
actually doesn't matter which way we compute our statistics, they give
mathematically the same result.

On a practical level, we usually resort to mutation-based computation, which is
how _slendr_ statistical functions operate by default. But population genetics
theory (described in the paper in detail) suggests that branch-based computation
is less noisy than mutation-based computation.

Let's test to what degree is this the case.

---

**Modify your `ts_replicate()` command so that it internally produces two data
frames:**

1. **`df_mutations` --- computed with `ts_f4()` same as before, except that you
should add a new column to this data frame called `mode` with the value `"mutataions"`,**

2. **`df_branches` --- computed with `ts_f4()` by additionally setting its
argument `mode = "branch"`, and adding a new column to this data frame called `mode` with the value `"branches"`.**

**The last thing your `ts_replicate()` command should do is to combine them into
a single data frame with `rbind(df_mutations, df_branches)`.**

**Now visualize the distributions of $f_4$` values between the two variations of
`ts_f4()` computation you just did. Is one of them noisier than the other? If
so, why could this be?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's the complete modified script `f_statistics.R` with the expanded solution
to this exercise:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p4 <- population("p4", time = 4000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 5), list(p2, 5), list(p3, 2), list(p4, 1))

df_comparison <- ts_replicate(
  n = 20, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  s <- ts_names(model, split = TRUE, schedule = schedule)

  df_mutations <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
  df_mutations$mode <- "mutations"

  df_branches <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch")
  df_branches$mode <- "branches"

  rbind(df_mutations, df_branches)
})
```

Let's visualize the results for comparison between mutation-based and
branch-based computation:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(mode, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ mode, scales = "free_y")
```

Do you see a massive difference in the variance between both batches of
simulations? I personally don't. This suggests that, particularly because it
makes comparisons of our simulations to real-world software methods (which all
work on mutations) easier, in a general case we might as well stick to
mutation-based computation.

See [this
tutorial](https://tskit.dev/tutorials/no_mutations.html#genealogy-based-measures-are-less-noisy)
(and particularly the directly linked section) for more explanation on this
topic.

:::



## Segregating sites and sequencing effort

Imagine you're in a situation, in which you want to decide how much sequencing
effort (i.e., how many individuals to sequence) in order to capture as much
genomic variation in your population of interest... while, at the same time, get
an idea of the point at which would you reach diminishing returns---in other
words, beyond what number of sequenced individuals would additional sequencing
wouldn't pay off anymore.

Motivation: Single model, repeated computation on a subset of tree-sequence samples.

What if you wanted to get a good idea of a genetic diversity in your population,
or another summary statistic?

```{r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)

library(slendr)
init_env()

pop <- population("pop", time = 1000, N = 10000)
model <- compile_model(pop, generation_time = 1, direction = "backward")
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>% ts_mutate(1e-8)

ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = "pop_1")
ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_2"))
ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = c("pop_1", "pop_2", "pop_3"))

# oh no, a mistake, we forgot to group this
ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = list(group = "pop_1"))
ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = list(group = c("pop_1", "pop_2")))
ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = list(group = c("pop_1", "pop_2", "pop_3")))

paste0("pop_", 1:3)

ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = list(group = paste0("pop_", 1:5)))

subset_segsites <- function(ts, i) {
  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), i)

  df <- ts_segregating(ts, sample_sets = list(group = subset))
  df$subset_n <- i

  df
}

subset_segsites(ts, 5)
```


```{r}
subset_n <- c(1:25, 50, 750, 100, 250, 500, 750, 1000, 2500, 5000, 7500, 10000)
subset_n

df <- map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_segsites(ts, .x))

ggplot(df, aes(subset_n, segsites)) + geom_point()
```

```{r}
subset_n <- c(1:25, 50, 750, 100, 250, 500, 750, 1000)

subset_diversity <- function(ts, i) {
  subset <- sample(ts_names(ts), i)

  df <- ts_diversity(ts, sample_sets = list(group = subset))
  df$subset_n <- i

  df
}

df <- map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x))

ggplot(df, aes(subset_n, diversity)) + geom_point() + scale_x_continuous()

ggplot(df, aes(subset_n, diversity)) + geom_point() + scale_x_log10()
```


```{r}
df <- rbind(
  map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x)),
  map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x)),
  map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x)),
  map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x)),
  map_dfr(subset_n, ~ subset_diversity(ts, .x))
)

ggplot(df, aes(subset_n, diversity)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + scale_x_continuous()

ggplot(df, aes(subset_n, diversity)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + scale_x_log10()

ggplot(df, aes(factor(subset_n), diversity)) + geom_boxplot()
```
